items.followUp: A force of 80 N acts at 60° to the x-axis. Find its x- and y-components.

rubric.why: Identifies the force and angle, and uses component resolution.
rubric.description: States the given force and angle and the component formula.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the given values and a correct component formula such as Fx = F cos θ or Fy = F sin θ.

rubric.why: The x-component is the adjacent component to the given angle.
rubric.how: Award 2 marks for the correct method and result, Fx = 50 cos 30° = 43.3 N.

rubric.why: The y-component is the opposite component to the given angle.
rubric.how: Award 2 marks for the correct method and result, Fy = 50 sin 30° = 25 N.

modelAnswer: Given: F = 50 N, θ = 30°
Fx = F cos θ
Fy = F sin θ
The components are 43.3 N along the x-axis and 25 N along the y-axis.

items.followUp: Estimate the number of seconds in 20 years.

rubric.why: An estimated year is taken as 365 days.
rubric.description: Uses the approximate number of days in a year.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for using 365 days per year (or an equivalent reasonable year length).

rubric.why: Converts years to seconds using days, hours, minutes and seconds.
rubric.description: Gives the estimated age in seconds.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a result close to 4.7 × 10^8 s with working consistent with the estimate.

modelAnswer: Given: t = 15 years
1 year ≈ 365 days; 1 day = 24 h; 1 h = 60 min; 1 min = 60 s

items.followUp: Why can a passenger move forward when a moving bus stops suddenly?

rubric.why: Inertia explains why the body resists a change in its state of motion.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the danger is due to inertia.

rubric.why: The passenger tends to keep moving when the bus changes motion suddenly.
rubric.description: Explains how the passenger may be thrown or fall from the roof.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for explaining that sudden starting, stopping or turning can make the passenger fall from the roof.

modelAnswer: It is dangerous because of inertia.
If the bus starts, stops or turns suddenly, a person on its roof tends to continue in the previous state of motion and may fall off.

items.followUp: Why does a piece of iron sink in water while a piece of wood may float?

rubric.why: A floating wood block has lower average density than water.
rubric.description: Compares the density of wood with that of water.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that wood is less dense than water (or has density less than water).

rubric.why: The upward buoyant force balances the block's weight when it floats.
rubric.description: Relates floating to the upward force of water.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for explaining that the upthrust balances the block's weight.

modelAnswer: A wood block floats because its average density is less than the density of water.
The upthrust exerted by water balances the weight of the block when it floats.

items.followUp: A 20 cm spanner is used to turn a nut with a perpendicular force of 150 N. Find the torque.

rubric.why: The distance from the pivot must be expressed in SI units for the calculation.
rubric.description: Converts the spanner length to metres.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for using r = 0.15 m.

rubric.why: For a perpendicular force, torque is force multiplied by perpendicular distance from the pivot.
rubric.description: Uses the torque formula and gives the correct result.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for τ = Fr = 200 × 0.15 = 30 N m.

modelAnswer: Given: F = 200 N, r = 15 cm = 0.15 m
For a perpendicular force, torque τ = Fr
τ = 30 N m

items.followUp: Define the centre of mass and show it on a uniform rectangular sheet.

rubric.why: The centre of mass is the point at which the body's mass can be considered concentrated.
rubric.description: Gives the definition of centre of mass.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for defining the centre of mass as the point where the whole mass of a body may be considered concentrated.

rubric.why: For a uniform rectangle, the centre of mass lies at the intersection of its diagonals.
rubric.description: Shows the centre of mass correctly on a labelled diagram.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a rectangle labelled 4 cm by 2 cm, with both diagonals drawn and their intersection labelled CM.

modelAnswer: The centre of mass is the point at which the whole mass of a body may be considered concentrated.
Draw a rectangle 4 cm long and 2 cm wide.
Draw both diagonals from corner to opposite corner.
Label their intersection CM (centre of mass).

items.followUp: Can a component of a vector be equal to its resultant? Explain briefly.

rubric.why: The resultant is the magnitude of the vector, while a component is its projection along an axis.
The resultant magnitude is at least as large as either rectangular component.
rubric.description: Justifies the answer using the relation between components and resultant.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that R = √(Ax² + Ay²), so a component cannot exceed R.

modelAnswer: No, a rectangular component cannot be greater than the resultant vector.
Since R = √(Ax² + Ay²), the magnitude of either component is less than or equal to R.

items.followUp: Describe one everyday example of thermal equilibrium.

rubric.why: Thermal equilibrium is reached when bodies in thermal contact have the same temperature.
rubric.description: States the condition for thermal equilibrium.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the bodies reach the same temperature.

rubric.why: A daily-life example should show heat transfer ending once temperatures equalise.
rubric.description: Gives a relevant everyday example and relates it to heat transfer.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for an example such as a spoon warming in hot tea until both reach the same temperature.

modelAnswer: For example, when a spoon is placed in hot tea, heat flows from the tea to the spoon.
After some time they reach the same temperature and there is no net heat flow; they are in thermal equilibrium.
